segments.narration: Parliament soaked its curtains in lime to survive the smell. London, summer 1858. The Thames was the city's open sewer.
Three million people, about two hundred thousand cesspits, and 360 sewers all emptying into the river. Then June hit thirty-six degrees and the water dropped.
Officials seriously discussed moving the government to Oxford, or to St Albans. Nothing concentrates a legislature like a smell it cannot escape.
A bill went in on the fifteenth of June and was law by the second of August. Joseph Bazalgette got three million pounds and built eighty-two miles of interceptor sewers.
It took 318 million bricks and eleven hundred miles of street sewers. London's last cholera outbreak was 1866, and the thing still runs.

verdicts.claim: During the summer of 1858 the curtains on the river side of the Palace of Westminster were soaked in chloride of lime to block the smell of the Thames.

verdicts.claim: Disraeli tabled the Metropolis Local Management Amendment Bill on 15 June 1858 and it became law on 2 August 1858, letting the Metropolitan Board of Works borrow three million pounds; Joseph Bazalgette's scheme included 82 miles of main interceptor sewers.
verdicts.note: 78% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 4 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Bazalgette's system used 318 million bricks and about 1,100 miles of street sewers, and the 1866 outbreak was London's last cholera outbreak.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives 318 million bricks, about 1,100 miles of street sewers feeding the interceptors, and the 1866 outbreak with 5,596 deaths as the last cholera outbreak in the capital, with the system still in operation. Secondary accounts of the sewer scheme corroborate the brick figure.
